stdout_tail:
Done. `analysis.py` and `result.json` are in the working directory.

## Finding (H1): yes — but the effect is two-tiered

**Held-out test ROC-AUC** (stratified 80/20, n=9,769; identical feature matrix for every learner, so differences are attributable to the learner):

| Model | test AUC | acc | F1(>50K) | PR-AUC | Brier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gradient boosting (HGB) | **0.9283** | 0.874 | 0.711 | 0.831 | 0.088 |
| Random forest | 0.9173 | 0.865 | 0.683 | 0.806 | 0.095 |
| MLP (100,50) | 0.9093 | 0.856 | 0.673 | 0.775 | 0.100 |
| Logistic regression | 0.9058 | 0.853 | 0.663 | 0.767 | 0.102 |
| Extra trees / tree(d=8) / k-NN | 0.90–0.895 | | | | |
| Gaussian naive Bayes | 0.8166 | 0.597 | 0.524 | 0.503 | 0.400 |
| Unpruned decision tree | 0.7716 | 0.820 | 0.631 | 0.508 | 0.170 |

**Primary metric: HGB − LogReg = +0.0226 AUC.** Among sensibly-specified families the gaps are real but modest (~0.01–0.02 AUC; every metric gives the same ordering). Across the full set of families the spread is 0.157 AUC — so family choice matters most through *avoiding a bad fit* (naive Bayes' independence assumption, an unregularised tree) than through the margin between the good options.

**Stability check.** 5×5 repeated stratified CV on all 48,842 rows with a different seed (12345) than the primary split, plus a 2,000-resample bootstrap on the test set. The finding held: HGB − LogReg = +0.0228, 95% CI [+0.0221, +0.0235], p=4e-29, HGB ahead in **25/25** folds; bootstrap +0.0226 [+0.0196, +0.0258]. HGB also beat RF in 25/25 folds (+0.0110). The family ordering was identical in every check.

Two judgment calls another researcher might make differently: I dropped `fnlwgt` (a census sampling weight, not a person-level predictor), and I spent no tuning budget per family — near-default hyperparameters throughout. Tuning would most plausibly help logistic regression, since its deficit here is largely unmodelled interactions (explicit interaction/spline terms could close part of the 0.02).

One environment note: the Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Drive connectors need authorization via your claude.ai connector settings before their tools are usable — irrelevant to this task, but they surfaced as unauthenticated.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the size of the effect depends on which families are compared. Among well-specified families the differences are real yet modest: gradient boosting reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 versus 0.906 for logistic regression (+0.022) and 0.917 for random forest - a consistent but small edge. Across the wider set of families the spread is large (0.16 AUC): Gaussian naive Bayes (0.817) and an unpruned decision tree (0.772) trail badly, so model family matters most through avoiding a poor choice rather than through the gap between good ones.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (HistGradientBoosting - Logistic Regression), held-out test set
parsed_result.direction: HGB > RF > LogReg > NaiveBayes > single tree; gradient boosting best, gap over logistic regression small (~0.02 AUC) but consistent
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Dropped fnlwgt (census sampling weight, not a person-level predictor); kept the 52 duplicate rows. Missing workclass/occupation/native-country encoded as an explicit 'Missing' level rather than dropping ~7% of rows. One-hot encoding (min_frequency=10, unknown ignored) plus median imputation for all models, with standardisation only for the scale-sensitive learners (LogReg, k-NN, MLP, NB) - trees got the identical feature matrix so differences are attributable to the learner. Stratified 80/20 split, seed 0. No class-imbalance reweighting and no threshold tuning; ROC-AUC chosen as the primary metric precisely because it is threshold-free (accuracy, F1, PR-AUC and Brier reported alongside and give the same ordering). Near-default hyperparameters, no tuning budget spent per family (HGB max_iter=400 lr=0.1; RF/ET 500 trees min_samples_leaf=3; LogReg L2 C=1; k=25 for k-NN; MLP 100-50 with early stopping). A tuning search could narrow or widen the gaps somewhat, and would most plausibly help logistic regression via explicit interaction/spline terms.
parsed_result.verification_method: (1) 5x5 repeated stratified cross-validation over the full 48,842 rows with a different seed (12345) from the primary split, giving 25 paired per-fold AUCs per family plus a paired t-test/CI on the fold-level differences; (2) 2000-resample bootstrap 95% CI of the pairwise test-set AUC differences on the held-out 20%.
parsed_result.verification_result: The finding held. In 5x5 repeated CV on the full data the HGB - LogReg AUC gap was +0.0228 (95% CI [+0.0221, +0.0235], p=4.1e-29), with HGB ahead in 25/25 folds; the test-set bootstrap gave +0.0226 (95% CI [+0.0196, +0.0258]). HGB also beat random forest in 25/25 folds (+0.0110). The ordering of families was identical in every check, and the large deficits of naive Bayes and the unpruned tree reproduced. Revised estimate of the headline gap: ~+0.02 AUC (0.015-0.025), i.e. statistically unambiguous but practically modest.
